title: A Strange Certainty
text:
For many years, often

I have remembered you, or your image,

to be more exact, since of what

we once loved there remains only

(as with a book) a very vague

general impression and some anecdote.

And often too I have wondered,

searching through the fog of memory

for I do not know whether an answer,

what you left in me

that is still mine,

and whether it was not love, my love for you,

and not you yourself, that still matters to me,

and what I still seek when I remember you.

If our life burns, are we flame

or what is burned and becomes ash?

In that excess which is time,

love and oblivion find their reason,

but not their measure. Remembering you,

I understand it so well that it matters little

to know or not to know, but only

to feel that you were part of myself,

that you are inside me, like my dreams,

which are and are not me, but are born in me,

that never again can you be erased from me,

and that, whether or not I want oblivion,

you must go on living with my life.

What a strange sensation, that certainty.


From "Espejos" 1986-1991

Pre-Textos, 1991 Valencia, Spain
editorial_note: The translation keeps the meditation's slow argument and the central flame-or-ash question.

title: Night Has Not Yet Come
text:
Night has not yet come,

and already it is night in this room

where yesterday the whole world fit,

and today there is no room for the two of us,

only for the night, already late, without end.
editorial_note: The contradiction between clock-time and emotional night is kept plain and compressed.

title: Snowfall
text:
Over the fields and over the streets,

silent and light,

turning in outline, the snow

falls.


In a thousand motionless forms,

on roofs and on roads,

on posts and in gardens,

it sleeps.


Its white skirt dances,

graceful in the wide sky,

then settles on the earth,

tired.


All around is peace,

shut in deep oblivion;

indifferent, the world

is silent.


But in the immense calm

the heart returns to memories

and thinks

of a quiet love.
editorial_note: The short final verbs are preserved to keep the falling, sleeping, and silencing motion.

title: The Stranger
text:
The stranger passing by

who still finds you worthy

of a fleeting word of desire,

perhaps because in the shadow of May's sweet night

your eyes still shine,

your slight gliding figure is still twenty years old,

does not know that you were

loved by the one you loved,

loved in the full and proud

delight of love,

and that in you there is not the smallest corner of flesh

or atom of the soul

that does not bear a mark of love.

He does not know that you lived only

to love the one who loved you,

and that even if you wished it,

no one could tear from you

that garment woven by love.

He, ignorant,

in you no longer beautiful, in you no longer young,

salutes the grace of the god:

breathes, as he passes,

in you already withered, in you abandoned,

the precious fragrance of the god.
editorial_note: The repeated in you remains visible, preserving the poem's ceremony of recognition and loss.

title: When One Night You Came to Her Bed...
text:
When one night you came to her bed,

and in the darkness murmured softly to her,

already bending over her: I cannot see you, I feel you,

and seized her with eagle claws,

and crushed her wholly in your exaltation,

molding her to yourself with such fury

that She lost the consciousness of existing...

do you remember?... And the two mouths were one

and one the spasm...

And the two lives fused in the perfect rhythm...


. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .


Through the open balcony,

the night looked on through the eyes of a blushing star...

And the sleep that followed resembled death,

and motionless as corpses,

the sadness of shadow watched over them until dawn.


Il libro di Mara, 1919
editorial_note: The erotic intensity is translated without euphemism while smoothing an obvious source typo in the phrase one the spasm.

title: The Silence
text:
Even in your taciturn anger She loved you...


when you shut yourself within yourself,

as in armor bristling with spikes,


as behind a bronze door

guarded by seven keys.


Resigned, without protest,

her heart wrung with anguish,

she suffered your long silences,


daring only to follow your steps

with her own, padded with shadows...


scarcely daring furtive caresses

with her brief light hand,

softer the harder the amorous yoke

that bound her to you...


But the expression of your anger, Beloved,

does not dissolve; lost are

the keys that close the bronze door...


In vain the little hand

knocks night and day at the door,


for merciless and eternal

is the silence of your tomb.


Il libro di Mara, 1919
editorial_note: The translation keeps the capitalized She and Beloved, preserving the elegiac drama of the address.

title: My Youth
text:
I have not lost you. You have remained

in the depths of my being. It is you, yet you are another:

without foliage or flower, without the bright laughter

you had in the time that does not return,

without that song. You are another, more beautiful.

You love, and do not hope to be loved: before

each flower that opens or fruit that ripens,

or little child born, to the God of fields

and lineages you give thanks from the heart.

Year after year, within yourself, you changed

face and substance. Each sorrow made you

firmer: against each footprint of passing

time, your hidden green sap

you set as remedy. Now you look at the light

that does not deceive; in its mirror you contemplate

enduring life. And you remain

like an age without a name: human

among human miseries, yet living

only from God and only in God happy.


O timeless youth, O ever

renewed hope, I entrust you

to those who will come, so that on earth

spring may blossom again, and in the sky

stars may be born when the sun goes down.


"Mia giovinezza"
editorial_note: The translation keeps the devotional turn of the later stanzas and the apostrophe to youth.

title: Mischiefs of the Verb
text:
I have the memory

of a memory

where everything was the face of dew,

intimate sun between the fingers,

river brought to its knees

to receive a caress.

I have the memory

of a memory

where you were precise and pure,

and now it is the poem

that invites you to suicide

because, as I breathe,

I invent you and invent you and invent you,

and you lose us both

by reinventing yourself.
editorial_note: The repeated invent keeps the poem's self-accusing spiral around language and desire.

title: The Distrustful Gods
text:
"No, no," said the gods,

"if there must be an eye,

let it belong to the mountain."

"No, no," said the gods,

"if there must be laughter,

let us offer it to the ocean so it may be cheered.

The word for the turkey,

for the cactus, for the brook!

And thought,

let the rock take possession of it

so as to recognize itself better."

"No, no," said the gods,

"let us spare ourselves

the human error."
editorial_note: The tone stays mythic and wry, with the gods distributing faculties away from humanity.

title: Bird
text:
You are nothing but the comma

of a sentence in the sky.

Is it not truly ridiculous,

this feigned world:

the palm tree with wings,

the eloquent desert,

the waterfall that bleats,

the tiger made volcano?

Richness is poverty!

The plump moons

are always poorly fed.

You return to my verses

where you were born, comma

become a crazed eagle

that circles and circles

and falls upon my neck.
editorial_note: Comma anchors the conceit: the bird begins as punctuation and returns as a dangerous image.

title: You Who Have Spent Everything
text:
You who have spent everything,

you who have destroyed everything:

it is glory to be the wind

and bliss to be the stone.

That tree grows green again,

that horse you condemned to silence

says what it thinks,

the waterfall recovers its true face

and the sky its size.

It is glory to be mud; coronation,

the oblivion

of a beetle gnawing its legs.

Look at them, they are better than you:

animals, twilights,

flint, forget-me-nots:

all of them raise

a monument to man

without carving an insult.
editorial_note: The direct address and paradoxes are kept sharp, especially the poem's reversal of human prestige.
